title: Choosing a water-efficient showerhead
subtitle: How to select and fit a low-flow showerhead without reducing comfort
excerpt: A standard shower uses 8 to 12 litres of hot water per minute. A well-designed water-efficient showerhead delivers 6 to 8 litres per minute with similar pressure and spray feel by aerating the flow. Switching to a rated low-flow head saves a typical household 10,000 to 20,000 litres of hot water per year. The choice between aerating and non-aerating heads, the compatibility with different pressure systems, and the impact on perceived comfort determine whether the saving is real or illusory.
sourceNotes: Waterwise UK shower water use data 2024. Defra Water Efficiency Product Labelling Scheme guidance. Methven, Neoperl, and Methven showerhead technical specifications.

glossaryTerms.definition: The volume of water a showerhead delivers per minute, measured in litres per minute (l/min). Standard: 8–12 l/min. Efficient: 6–8 l/min. Ultra-low: 4–6 l/min (typically requires high pressure to work well).

content.text: An average UK shower runs for 8 minutes. At 10 litres per minute, that is 80 litres of water per shower, and most of it is hot, requiring energy to heat. A household with two daily showers uses 58,400 litres of hot water per year from the shower alone. Fitting a 6 litre/minute head reduces that by 14,600 litres, saving meaningful amounts on hot water heating each year.
Low-flow showerheads need a minimum water pressure to work correctly. UK homes have two main supply types:

High-pressure system (combi boiler or mains-pressure cylinder): dynamic pressure typically 1.0 to 3.0 bar at the showerhead. Any water-efficient showerhead rated for 0.5 bar or higher will work well. The aerating mechanism creates a full, high-volume feel at these pressures.

Low-pressure system (cold water tank in loft plus hot water cylinder): dynamic pressure typically 0.1 to 0.5 bar at shower height. Most standard low-flow aerating heads require 0.5 bar minimum. At 0.1 to 0.3 bar, a gravity-rated showerhead is needed, these typically have larger nozzle holes and a wider spray pattern to work at low pressure. Fitting a standard aerating head on a gravity system produces a trickle.
To estimate shower pressure without a gauge, hold a 1-litre jug under the current showerhead for exactly 6 seconds. The volume collected multiplied by 10 gives the approximate
in litres per minute. Divide by 60 and multiply by static head (height in metres from tank base to showerhead) for rough pressure: at 0.1 bar per metre, 3 m head = 0.3 bar.
Turn off the shower mixer valve. Unscrew the existing showerhead from the hose or fixed arm using an adjustable spanner. Protect the chrome finish with a cloth between the jaws.
Wrap two turns of PTFE tape clockwise around the thread of the new showerhead. Screw on by hand until snug, then one-eighth turn further with the spanner.
Run the shower and check for leaks at the fitting for 30 seconds. If dripping at the thread, add another half turn. Do not overtighten, the brass or plastic thread can crack.

If the new head produces a noticeably less satisfying spray on a high-pressure system, the head's aerating nozzles may be partially clogged with limescale. Soak the showerhead in white wine vinegar for 2 hours and flush. In very hard water areas (above 300 mg/l), descaling every 3 to 6 months maintains performance.
